The flood limits shown on the map reflect channel conditions that existed when the floods occurred and no attempt has been made to appraise the effect of channel changes that may have been made later. Protective works that were built after the flood of 1957 may reduce the frequency of flooding in the area but will not necessarily eliminate all future flooding.
Exhibits "20" to "28" are excerpts from two reports by the Department of the Interior, United States Geological Survey; (1) Floods in Steqer Quadrangle, Northeastern Illinois, Hydrologic Investigations Atlas HA-209, by Howard E. Allen in 1966 and (2) Floods in Harvey Quadrangle, Illinois, Hydrologic Investigations Atlas HA-90, by Howard E. Allen and V. Jeff May in 1964.
Gage heights for crest-stage gages located in the Steger and Harvey quadrangles can be converted to elevations above mean sea level by adding the gage height to the appropriate datum of the gage, listed in Exhibit "21". The size of the drainage area for each gage also is shown in this Exhibit. Drainage divides are shown on Exhibit "20".
The rate of flood discharge of a stream is the volume of flow that passes a particular location in a given period of time. Discharge rates usually are expressed in cubic feet per second (cfs). Peak discharge, the maximum discharge attained by a flood, generally occurs at the time of the maximum height (stage) of the flood, but if a stream is affected by variable backwater, the time of the peak discharge may not coincide with that of the maximum stage. For example, backwater from a debris or ice jam may cause a high stage during a period of relatively low discharge. Exhibit "22 " shows the frequency of flood discharges on Thorn Creek at Glenwood and Butterfield Creek at Flossmoor. Exhibit "23 " also shows the relation between the frequency of flood stage. Exhibit "24 " shows the recurrence intervals for Thorn Creek at Glenwood and Butterfield Creek at Flossmoor, Illinois.
